newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP launches bill to set immigration quota.
newsitem.headline: German FDP launches bill to set immigration quota.

text.p: Germany's liberal Free Democrats, junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition, launched a bill on Thursday to set quotas on the number of foreigners allowed into the country.
"Immigration must be orientated to our own interests so that Germany profits from it socially and economically," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told a news conference.

Germany does not officially accept immigration by foreigners from outside the European Union, but every year it takes in tens of thousands of asylum seekers, and people of German descent from former Soviet republics and eastern Europe.

The FDP said the bill would reduce immigration to Germany overall, and give preference to people who could do particular jobs or with particular skills. It would also set quotas for ethnic Germans and migrant workers allowed into Germany.
Over seven million foreigners live in Germany, many from Turkey, Italy and former Yugoslavia who were invited as "guest workers" during West Germany's post-war economic boom.

Record unemployment has prompted leading conservatives to call for stricter controls on asylum seekers and migrant workers from outside the EU. But they reject FDP's proposals for a formal law, which they say would make immigration easier.
Westerwelle denied this was the case. "The FDP does not want more immigration, but more control over immigration," he said.

The FDP said an important part of the bill were rules to govern the systematic integration of immigrants, including compulsory language courses, which all applicants for German citizenship would have to attend and pass.

The bill would also extend citizenship automatically to many foreigners born in Germany and those who have lived here for longer than eight years. The current rules for citizenship rely overwhelmingly on blood lines.

But the proposal faces stiff opposition from within the ruling coalition. The FDP said it hoped to prompt dialogue and did not want to force the law through parliament with the support of opposition parties against the coalition's will.

Westerwelle said if politicians in Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and their arch-conservative Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), refused to consider the proposal they would damage relations with their FDP partners.
"Reservations among the CDU and CSU are not tenable. It is high time we tackled this topic in an unbiased way," said FDP deputy leader Cornelia Schmalz-Jacobsen.
But both the CDU and the CSU swiftly emphasised their opposition to the bill.

"There will be no immigration law with the CDU/CSU," CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said. "All the positive expectations that are linked to such a legal initiative would become negative in reality."
The CSU's home affairs spokesman Wolfgang Zeitlmann said the FDP's plans could not work and would create legal and constitutional problems.
Hintze agreed, adding that a change in immigration law without a change to the asylum law would be senseless.

Asylum requests have fallen sharply since 1993 when Bonn tightened what were previously Europe's most liberal asylum laws to stop an influx of refugees, but some conservatives want further limits on asylum.
